Tonight we went to a local club with the P.A.A. No. 1,,
Max Lessner, who used to be with CNAC in Shanghai.
He was born in
Japan, his father was Rumanian, his mother Russian. He is now a
British citizen.
He married a white Russian who was born in Harbin
and raised in Shanghai - very charming•
Our party at the club -
a "ecktail dance" was about as assorted in nationalities as the
pedigree of our host.
Indian officers in the British dress uniform
(minus the crown on the shoulder) some of whom were stunning and
Hebe nearly lost her eyesight.
Members of the diplomatic corps
from all over the world. It was really a treat.
The Lessners had
invited a very attractive young Britisher for Hebe and the evening
was a great success. We had a fine dinner in the Club grill and
came home reasonably early.
Must go to bed now for an early start
tomorrow morning to Agra.
н. м. В.

(Family Letter No. 2)
Enroute Damascus-Istanbul
January 10, 1950
Dear Family,
We're now backtracking a bit - about 800 miles to be
more specific.
We had originally planned this one day in Constan-
tinople - a name you older ones will know better than Istanbul. -
but when I found that there was a long waiting list of pay pass-
engers I cancelled our trip.
However, this morning the office
the truth because there are three empty seats on the plane.
This morning in Damascus we visited the best shop in the
Debby and Hebe shopped amid a million things which anyone
would crave while I went to call on the American Consul - sort of
a command performance where there are few Americans. He, in common
with most other well informed, is worried over the Palestine quarrel
between the Jews and Arabs.
It is thought that no matter what
promises the Jews may make to the U.N. that they will not be sat-
isfied until they have taken all of Palestine. Meanwhile, the
Arabs of Palestine are trying to join what they have left of their
country to Trans-Jordan, calling the combination "Jordan". Our
guide said that P.A.A. was much disliked in Syria a few years ago
because someone (probably T.W.A.) started a rumor: that all of our
of most over-done propaganda, it wasn't long before enough P.A.A.
McPherson, to convince the Syrians they had been misinformed. There
are about 4,000,000 people in Syria of whom two-thirds are Moslem
and one-third Christian; a very few Jews, most of the latter having
gone to Israel.
This whole section of the world is like a smoul-
dering fire and may burst into flame at any time.
Istanbul
January 11, 1950
Istanbul. We landed at about 10:00 p.m. and drove into
town with
the P.A.A. No. l. He apologized for not getting us into
the best hotel, but we are delighted with the Pera Palace.
and I have a red draped bedroom with a twelve foot ceiling; the
room is filled with German furniture of the 190's; a bathroom
larger than the average bedroom - slightly on the cold side on
account of because one window is broken and the paper in lieu of
glass is loose at the bottom; a living room done in brocade panels
with heevy framed Germanic paintings, four high windows complete
with heavy twelve foot drapes and more ponderous German furniture.
I'm sure that the Kaiser must have stayed here when
he visited
Turkey in 1899.
(Found out later that he did!) We're waiting now
for a car and guide.
Outside it is snowing, but the snow melts as
it hits.
A string of cars moves by in constant procession three
floors below, and each driver leans on the horn continually.
Debby says each minute is like New Year's Eve.
It's now 9:30 a.m.
and we're anxious to get going for if the plane from London is on
-1-

-2-
schedule this will be our only day in Istanbul.
Iwo days later
We made the rounds of Istanbul including the lamous mosque
of St. Sophia.
Hebe knew all about it from her college training and
of course it was a great day for her.
It is the third largest church
in the world - outranked only by St. Peters in Rome and St. Pauls
in London.
Near St. Sochia is the smaller but I think more beautiful
Blue Mosque which has six minarets instead of the conventional four
because of a mistake in the specifications.
We also took in the ex-
Sultan's palace and saw there the finest collection of Chinese porcelain
in the world.
Chinese celadons by the hundreds, each one of which in
itself would be prized by most museums. It seems that many of the old
Sultans ordered lots of china for their extensive kitchens and stored
it in the "cellar".
The next Sultan ordered more quite unaware of the
stock already on hand.
(Governments have a way of doing that!) In
the reconstruction of the ancient kitchens great numbers of cases of
this porcelain were unearthed and formed this magnificent collection
consisting of pieces from the 14th Century through the 18th.
We drove around Istanbul and out toward Roberts College
along the shore of the Bosphorus.
We had lunch at a famous plane
in the heart of the old city called Pandilla. It is reached
up a narrow, dirty alley.
Cabinet Ministers and leading businessmen
tread the alley to get the best food in the Middle East.
The owner,
Pandilla, is a show in himself, standing behind a slightly elevated
counter directing the whole operstion, greeting his customers as they
come and go, shouting orders through a small window to the kitchen
and directing his weiters around the small dining room.
Not a detail
missed his watchful check - the while he sipped brandy and became
more and more mellow as the hour advanced.
He gets up at 4:00 a.m.
and goes to the market where he buys the best of everything. He has
turned down hundreds of offers to open a better restaurant in Is-
tanbul as well as offers from New York, Paris,
etc. He says that
he is doing all right where he is and why move!
During the day the snow turned into a snowstorm and then
a blizzard. Our plane was late starting from Brussels but we went
out to the airport at 2:00 a.m.
the plane came in at 3:00 a.m. and
was serviced in a real blizzard, but eventually we were loaded on
board after Debby and Hebe had returned the werm clothes which we
had borrowed. We taxied out for the take-off and then taxied back
because number one engine - thet's the one on the left - wouldn't
run properly.
They struggled with it for a while and then postponed
the flight for repairs and crew rest.
We were taken in a bus to a
small hotel near the field and there we stayed all day while the
blizzard continued. Debby and Hebe bundled up in blankets off the
airplane. However, at 7:00 p.m. we did get away and had an un-
eventful
flight back to Damascus and on to here - Delhi - where we
arrived at noon local time on Friday the 13th.
lomorrow, Saturday, we are going to drive over to Agra,
about a four hour trip, to see the laj Mahal, stay in Agra overnight
and return Sunday night.
